## Finite-size scaling and renormalisation {#sec-finite-size-scaling}

Simulations run on finite lattices, where nothing is singular: the spanning probability rises smoothly, the susceptibility has a finite peak, and the strength of the largest
cluster never vanishes. Finite-size scaling turns this into information. Near the critical point the only length that matters is the correlation length $\xi \propto
\lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\nu}$, and a finite system of side $L$ behaves according to the ratio $L/\xi$; so curves for different $L$ collapse onto one when plotted against $(p -
p_c)L^{1/\nu}$, which determines $p_c$ and $\nu$ [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 4.6 and footnote 5]. Real-space renormalisation goes the other way: it
replaces blocks of sites by single sites, which divides $\xi$ by the block size, and the fixed points of the resulting map of parameters are the critical points
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 1.4.3]. This section defines finite-size scaling and proves the fixed points and the exponent of the simplest real-space
renormalisation of percolation. The Wilsonian renormalisation group of field theory is in the physics tutorial
([Renormalisation](../../fundamentals-of-theoretical-physics/renormalisation/index.qmd#sec-wilsonian-rg)).

For more on this topic, see @charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017 [Secs. 4.5-4.6], @bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021 [Sec. 1.4.3] and
@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018 [Sec. 3.3.1].

### Finite-size scaling

On a lattice of side $L$, an observable $Y$ that diverges like $\lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\kappa}$ in the infinite system cannot exceed a power of $L$, and its values near $p_c$ depend on
$p$ and $L$ only through $L/\xi$. The hypothesis makes this a functional form with two exponents and a scaling function, and it is what `data_collapse` of kind `'scaling'` fits. The
spanning probability, which tends to a step function, is the case without a prefactor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-finite-size-scaling}
#### Finite-size scaling hypothesis and data collapse

Let $Y_L(p)$ be an observable of a system of linear size $L$ near a critical point $p_c$ at which the correlation length diverges as $\xi \propto \lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\nu}$. The
observable obeys **finite-size scaling** with exponent $a$ if there is a function $\Phi$, the **scaling function**, such that
$$
Y_L(p) \approx L^a\,\Phi\bigl((p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}\bigr)
$$
for large $L$ and small $\lvert p - p_c\rvert$. Plotting $L^{-a}Y_L$ against $x = (p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}$ makes the curves of all sizes fall on the graph of $\Phi$, a **data collapse**. When $a = 0$, the curves of
different sizes **cross** at $p = p_c$, where all take the value $\Phi(0)$.
:::

::::

If $Y_\infty(p) \propto \lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\kappa}$, consistency for $L \gg \xi$ requires $\Phi(x) \propto \lvert x\rvert^{-\kappa}$ at large $\lvert x\rvert$, and then $L^a\lvert x\rvert^{-\kappa}$ must not depend
on $L$: $a = \kappa/\nu$. So the susceptibility peak grows like $L^{\gamma/\nu}$ and the strength at $p_c$ falls like $L^{-\beta/\nu}$. This is the scaling of two variables of
@exm-scaling-two-variables, applied to size and distance from the critical point.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spanning probability is dimensionless. It has $a = 0$, and its curves for different sizes cross near $p_c$ and sharpen as $L$ grows.

::: {#exm-fss-spanning-curves}
#### Spanning curves

@fig-percolation-fss shows $\Pi_L(p)$ for $L = 16$, $32$, $64$, $128$ and their collapse with $\nu = 4/3$. The width of the transition shrinks like $L^{-1/\nu} = L^{-3/4}$, so doubling $L$
narrows it by $2^{3/4} \approx 1.7$.

![Spanning probability of site percolation against $p$ for lattices of side $16$ to $128$ (left), and the same data against $(p - p_c)L^{3/4}$ (right), where the curves
collapse onto one.](figures/percolation_fss.svg){#fig-percolation-fss width=95%}
:::

The crossing points estimate $p_c$ without any exponent. `data_collapse` of kind `'crossings'` interpolates where the curves of consecutive sizes intersect.

::: {#exm-fss-crossings}
#### Crossings

From $300$ lattices per point, the crossings of $L = 16, 32, 64$ fall between $0.593$ and $0.598$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, data_collapse
rng, ps = np.random.default_rng(22), np.round(np.linspace(0.56, 0.62, 13), 3)
curves = {L: np.array([clusters(rng.random((300, L, L)) < p, kind="spanning").probability for p in ps]) for L in (16, 32, 64)}
print("crossings:", np.round(data_collapse(curves, kind="crossings", parameters=ps).crossings, 4).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
crossings: [0.5927, 0.5975]
```
:::

The collapse can be fitted. Minimising the spread of the rescaled curves over $p_c$ and $\nu$ gives both at once.

::: {#exm-fss-fit}
#### Fitting $p_c$ and $\nu$

`data_collapse(..., fit=("critical", "nu"))` starts from guesses and returns the values that collapse the curves best. With three small sizes and $300$ lattices per point they come out near
$0.596$ and $1.5$, within the combined statistical and finite-size errors of $0.5927$ and $4/3$; larger lattices bring them closer.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, data_collapse
rng, ps = np.random.default_rng(23), np.round(np.linspace(0.54, 0.64, 11), 3)
curves = {L: np.array([clusters(rng.random((300, L, L)) < p, kind="spanning").probability for p in ps]) for L in (16, 32, 64)}
result = data_collapse(curves, parameters=ps, critical=0.59, nu=1.3, fit=("critical", "nu"))
print(f"p_c = {result.critical:.4f}, nu = {result.nu:.3f}, quality {result.quality:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p_c = 0.5956, nu = 1.494, quality 0.0023
```
:::

The strength at $p_c$ decays with $L$. With $\beta = 5/36$ and $\nu = 4/3$ [@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Sec. 2.3, Fig. 2.8 and eq. (2.10)], $P_\infty(p_c) \propto L^{-\beta/\nu} = L^{-5/48}$, the same exponent as the mass ratio of @exr-perc-half, since $D_f = 2 - \beta/\nu$.

::: {#exm-fss-strength}
#### The strength at the threshold

The slow decay $L^{-0.104}$ explains why the share of occupied sites in the largest cluster stays near $0.45$ over the sizes of @exr-perc-half, although it tends to $0$.
:::

At the critical point the correlation length is the system size. Charbonneau's footnote puts it as the correlation length of a perturbation becoming comparable to the size of the
system [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 4.6, footnote 5].

::: {#exm-fss-xi-equals-l}
#### $\xi \approx L$

In a finite system, $\xi$ saturates at a value of order $L$ near $p_c$. The pseudo-critical point $p_L$ where an observable peaks satisfies $\xi(p_L) \approx L$, so $\lvert p_L - p_c\rvert \propto L^{-1/\nu}$:
finite systems show their transition shifted by an amount that vanishes like $L^{-3/4}$ for percolation and $L^{-1}$ for the Ising model.
:::

The Ising model obeys the same scaling. Its susceptibility peak grows like $L^{\gamma/\nu} = L^{7/4}$ in two dimensions, with $\gamma = 7/4$ and $\nu = 1$ (Thurner's Table 3.2)
[@thurnerIntroductionTheoryComplex2018, Sec. 3.3.1.1, Table 3.2].

::: {#exm-fss-ising-chi}
#### The susceptibility at $T_c$

At $h = 0$ on a finite lattice $\langle m\rangle = 0$, so the susceptibility per spin is $\chi/N = N\langle m^2\rangle/T$; at $T_c$ it grows like $L^{1.75}$ for $L = 8, 16, 32, 64$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
sizes, chi = (8, 16, 32, 64), []
for L in sizes:
    m = np.asarray(simulate(IsingSystem(L, temperature=2.269, random_state=29), until=20500, random_state=29).get_values("spins.spin"))[500:].mean(axis=1)
    chi.append(L * L * (m**2).mean() / 2.269)
print("chi/N:", np.round(chi, 2).tolist(), f"slope {scaling(np.column_stack([sizes, chi]), kind="allometric").exponent:.2f}, gamma/nu = 1.75")
```

```{.text .run-output}
chi/N: [18.15, 61.26, 213.62, 745.09] slope 1.79, gamma/nu = 1.75
```
:::

The Binder cumulant is the magnetic analogue of the spanning probability. $U_L = 1 - \langle m^4\rangle/(3\langle m^2\rangle^2)$ is dimensionless, tends to $\frac23$ in the ordered phase and to
$0$ in the disordered one, and its curves cross at $T_c$.

::: {#exm-fss-binder}
#### The Binder cumulant

Because $U_L$ has $a = 0$, it depends on $T$ and $L$ only through $(T - T_c)L^{1/\nu}$, and at $T_c$ it takes a size-independent value [@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Sec. 5.4, eqs. (5.14)-(5.19)], about $0.61$ for the two-dimensional Ising model on a
square torus. Its crossings are a standard estimator of $T_c$; an exercise computes them.
:::

Finite-size scaling explains why simulations of different sizes agree away from $p_c$ and disagree near it. Away from $p_c$, $\lvert x\rvert$ is large for all sizes, the curves are on their
asymptotes, and the size does not matter.

::: {#exm-fss-away}
#### Far from the threshold

At $p = 0.5$, $\xi$ is a few lattice spacings, $x = (p - p_c)L^{3/4}$ is large and negative for $L \geq 32$, and $\Pi_L \approx 0$ for every size; similarly at $p = 0.7$ every size spans. Only within
$\lvert p - p_c\rvert \lesssim L^{-3/4}$ do the curves differ, which is where @fig-percolation-fss shows them.
:::

Downey's estimate is independent of $n$ because it finds the crossing. His random walk targets $\Pi_n(q) = \frac12$, which by finite-size scaling is at $p_c + x_{1/2}n^{-3/4}$, so it converges to
$p_c$ [@downeyThinkComplexity2018, Ch. 7].

::: {#exm-fss-downey}
#### Why Downey's value does not depend on $n$

$\Pi_n(q) = \Phi((q - p_c)n^{3/4})$, and $\Phi(x_{1/2}) = \frac12$ with $x_{1/2}$ close to $0$ for square lattices, so the median of $\Pi_n$ is $p_c + O(n^{-3/4})$. For $n = 100$ the shift is below
the resolution $0.005$ of his walk, which is why he found $0.59$ for every $n$ he tried.
:::

Corrections to scaling limit the method. The hypothesis holds for large $L$; small lattices carry corrections of relative size $L^{-\omega}$ that shift crossings and spoil collapses.

::: {#exm-fss-corrections}
#### Corrections to scaling

The crossings of consecutive sizes drift towards $p_c$ as $L$ grows; extrapolating them in $L^{-1/\nu - \omega}$ removes most of the bias. With the sizes of these examples the drift is of the same order
as the statistical error, so a fit to all sizes at once, as in @exm-fss-fit, is adequate.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the consistency condition $a = \kappa/\nu$ stated after the definition. It is the step that relates finite-size exponents to infinite-system exponents.

::: {#exr-fss-consistency}
#### The exponent of the prefactor

Show that if $Y_\infty(p) = c\lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\kappa}$ and $Y_L(p) = L^a\Phi((p - p_c)L^{1/\nu})$ with $\Phi(x) \sim c\lvert x\rvert^{-\kappa}$ as $\lvert x\rvert \to \infty$, then $Y_L \to Y_\infty$ for fixed $p \neq p_c$ only
if $a = \kappa/\nu$, and that then $Y_L(p_c) \propto L^{\kappa/\nu}$. Check with $\Phi(x) = (1 + x^2)^{-\kappa/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For fixed $p \neq p_c$, $x = (p - p_c)L^{1/\nu} \to \pm\infty$, so $Y_L \approx L^ac\lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\kappa}L^{-\kappa/\nu}$, which has a finite nonzero limit iff $a = \kappa/\nu$, and the limit is then $Y_\infty$. At
$p_c$, $x = 0$ and $Y_L(p_c) = L^a\Phi(0)$.

## Python

The model scaling function with $\kappa = 2$, $\nu = 1$: $Y_L$ at a fixed $p$ approaches $Y_\infty$ and $Y_L(p_c)$ grows like $L^2$.

```{.python .run}
kappa, nu, d = 2.0, 1.0, 0.05
Y = lambda L, delta: L ** (kappa / nu) * (1 + (delta * L ** (1 / nu)) ** 2) ** (-kappa / 2)
print("Y_L at distance 0.05:", [round(Y(L, d), 2) for L in (10, 100, 1000)], "infinite system", round(d**-kappa, 2))
print("Y_L at p_c:", [Y(L, 0.0) for L in (10, 100, 1000)])
```

```{.text .run-output}
Y_L at distance 0.05: [80.0, 384.62, 399.84] infinite system 400.0
Y_L at p_c: [100.0, 10000.0, 1000000.0]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise measures the width of the transition. The interval where $\Pi_L$ rises from $0.1$ to $0.9$ shrinks like $L^{-1/\nu}$.

::: {#exr-fss-width}
#### The width of the transition

Estimate the $p$ at which $\Pi_L = 0.1$ and $0.9$ for $L = 16, 32, 64$ by interpolation on a grid of $p$, and fit the exponent of the width against $L$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\Pi_L(p) = \Phi((p - p_c)L^{1/\nu})$, so the two points are at $p_c + x_{0.1}L^{-1/\nu}$ and $p_c + x_{0.9}L^{-1/\nu}$, and the width is $(x_{0.9} - x_{0.1})L^{-1/\nu}$. The fitted slope should be near $-3/4$.

## Python

Interpolated quantiles of the spanning curves.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, scaling
rng, ps = np.random.default_rng(25), np.linspace(0.45, 0.75, 31)
sizes, widths = (16, 32, 64), []
for L in sizes:
    curve = np.maximum.accumulate([clusters(rng.random((200, L, L)) < p, kind="spanning").probability for p in ps])
    widths.append(np.interp(0.9, curve, ps) - np.interp(0.1, curve, ps))
print("widths:", np.round(widths, 4).tolist(), f"exponent {scaling(np.column_stack([sizes, widths]), kind="allometric").exponent:.2f}, -1/nu = -0.75")
```

```{.text .run-output}
widths: [0.1695, 0.0911, 0.0636] exponent -0.71, -1/nu = -0.75
```
::::
:::

The third exercise computes the Binder cumulant of @exm-fss-binder. Its crossings estimate the critical temperature of the Ising model.

::: {#exr-fss-binder}
#### Binder crossings

For $L = 8$ and $16$, compute $U_L = 1 - \langle m^4\rangle/(3\langle m^2\rangle^2)$ at $T = 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4$, and find the crossing by linear interpolation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For Gaussian $m$ (high temperature) $\langle m^4\rangle = 3\langle m^2\rangle^2$ and $U = 0$; for $m = \pm m_0$ (low temperature) $U = \frac23$. Between, $U_L$ is a function of $(T - T_c)L$, and the curves of two sizes cross near
$T_c = 2.269$.

## Python

The cumulants and their crossing with `data_collapse(kind="crossings")`.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import data_collapse
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem
temps, curves = np.array([2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4]), {}
for L in (8, 16):
    U = []
    for T in temps:
        m = np.asarray(simulate(IsingSystem(L, temperature=T, random_state=26), until=20500, random_state=26).get_values("spins.spin"))[500:].mean(axis=1)
        U.append(1 - (m**4).mean() / (3 * (m**2).mean() ** 2))
    curves[L] = np.array(U)
print({L: np.round(U, 3).tolist() for L, U in curves.items()}, "crossing:", np.round(data_collapse(curves, kind="crossings", parameters=temps).crossings, 3).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
{8: [0.647, 0.63, 0.607, 0.571], 16: [0.658, 0.639, 0.601, 0.516]} crossing: [2.263]
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise collapses the mean cluster size, an observable with $a \neq 0$. Its prefactor exponent is $\gamma_p/\nu = 43/24$.

::: {#exr-fss-mean-size}
#### Collapsing the mean cluster size

Compute $S_L(p)$ for $L = 32, 64$ on a grid of $p$ near $p_c$ and collapse $L^{-43/24}S_L$ against $(p - 0.5927)L^{3/4}$; report the quality of the collapse with the exponent given and with $a = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$S$ diverges with $\gamma_p = 43/18$, so by @exr-fss-consistency $a = \gamma_p/\nu = 43/24 \approx 1.79$. With the right $a$ the rescaled curves overlap near $p_c$; with $a = 0$ the curve of the larger lattice lies higher by a
factor $2^{1.79} \approx 3.5$, and the quality measure, the spread of the rescaled curves, is much worse.

## Python

Mean sizes with `clusters(kind="percolation")` and the quality from `data_collapse` with fixed exponents.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, data_collapse
rng, ps = np.random.default_rng(27), np.round(np.linspace(0.56, 0.62, 7), 3)
curves = {L: np.array([np.mean([clusters(rng.random((L, L)) < p, kind="percolation").mean_size for _ in range(40)]) for p in ps]) for L in (32, 64)}
for a in (43 / 24, 0.0):
    print(f"a = {a:.3f}: quality {data_collapse(curves, parameters=ps, critical=0.5927, nu=4 / 3, exponent=a).quality:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a = 1.792: quality 0.0342
a = 0.000: quality 0.9727
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise checks the shift of the pseudo-critical point, the claim of @exm-fss-xi-equals-l. The temperature of the susceptibility peak of the Ising model approaches $T_c$ like $L^{-1}$.

::: {#exr-fss-shift}
#### The shifted peak

For $L = 8$ and $16$, locate the maximum of $\chi/N = N\operatorname{Var}(\lvert m\rvert)/T$ on a grid $T = 2.25, 2.3, \dots, 2.6$, and compare the shifts $T_L - T_c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\chi_L(T) = L^{\gamma/\nu}\Phi((T - T_c)L)$ peaks where $\Phi$ does, at $x^* > 0$, so $T_L = T_c + x^*/L$: the shift halves when $L$ doubles. The grid limits the precision, but the peak of the smaller lattice lies
further above $T_c$.

## Python

The susceptibility on the grid for both sizes.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem
temps = np.round(np.arange(2.25, 2.61, 0.05), 2)
for L in (8, 16):
    chi = [L * L * np.abs(np.asarray(simulate(IsingSystem(L, temperature=T, random_state=28), until=10500, random_state=28).get_values("spins.spin"))[500:].mean(axis=1)).var() / T for T in temps]
    print(f"L = {L}: peak at T = {temps[int(np.argmax(chi))]}, shift {temps[int(np.argmax(chi))] - 2.269:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
L = 8: peak at T = 2.55, shift 0.281
L = 16: peak at T = 2.4, shift 0.131
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise compares two estimators of the susceptibility at $T_c$. The variance of $\lvert m\rvert$, which has a peak, and the second moment of $m$, which grows monotonically, scale with the same exponent.

::: {#exr-fss-gamma-nu}
#### Two susceptibilities

Show that $N\operatorname{Var}(\lvert m\rvert)/T$ and $N\langle m^2\rangle/T$ both scale like $L^{\gamma/\nu}$ at $T_c$, and compare their slopes for $L = 8, 16, 32$ from runs of $4 \times 10^4$ sweeps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

At $T_c$ the law of $mL^{\beta/\nu}$ tends to a fixed distribution, so $\langle m^2\rangle \propto L^{-2\beta/\nu}$ and $\operatorname{Var}\lvert m\rvert \propto L^{-2\beta/\nu}$ as well; times $N = L^2$ this is $L^{2 - 2\beta/\nu} = L^{\gamma/\nu}$ by the scaling relation
$\gamma/\nu = 2 - 2\beta/\nu = 7/4$. The variance of $\lvert m\rvert$ is a small difference of large terms and needs longer runs; its slope is noisier.

## Python

Both estimators from the same runs.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem
from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
sizes, var_abs, second = (8, 16, 32), [], []
for L in sizes:
    m = np.asarray(simulate(IsingSystem(L, temperature=2.269, random_state=32), until=40500, random_state=32).get_values("spins.spin"))[500:].mean(axis=1)
    var_abs.append(L * L * np.abs(m).var() / 2.269)
    second.append(L * L * (m**2).mean() / 2.269)
fit = lambda y: scaling(np.column_stack([sizes, y]), kind="allometric").exponent
print(f"slope of N Var|m|/T {fit(var_abs):.3f}, slope of N<m^2>/T {fit(second):.3f}, gamma/nu = 1.75")
```

```{.text .run-output}
slope of N Var|m|/T 1.986, slope of N<m^2>/T 1.712, gamma/nu = 1.75
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise collapses the Ising magnetisation, an observable with a negative prefactor exponent. With $\beta/\nu = 1/8$, $L^{1/8}\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle$ is a function of $(T - T_c)L$ only.

::: {#exr-fss-magnetisation}
#### Collapsing the magnetisation

For $L = 8, 16, 32$ and $T = 2.15, 2.2, \dots, 2.4$, compute $\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle$ and the quality of the collapse with $a = -1/8$, $\nu = 1$, $T_c = 2.269$, and with $T_c = 2.4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$m \propto (T_c - T)^\beta$ gives $a = -\beta/\nu = -1/8$. With the correct $T_c$ the rescaled curves overlap; with a wrong $T_c$ they do not, and the quality measure is larger. This is the principle of the fit in @exm-fss-fit.

## Python

The curves and the two qualities.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import data_collapse
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem
temps = np.round(np.arange(2.15, 2.41, 0.05), 2)
curves = {L: np.array([np.abs(np.asarray(simulate(IsingSystem(L, temperature=T, initial="up", random_state=30), until=6500, random_state=30).get_values("spins.spin"))[500:].mean(axis=1)).mean() for T in temps]) for L in (8, 16, 32)}
for Tc in (2.269, 2.4):
    print(f"T_c = {Tc}: quality {data_collapse(curves, parameters=temps, critical=Tc, nu=1.0, exponent=-0.125).quality:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
T_c = 2.269: quality 0.0002
T_c = 2.4: quality 0.0807
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise asks why the scaling variable is $(p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}$. It derives it from the requirement that only $L/\xi$ matters.

::: {#exr-fss-variable}
#### The scaling variable

Show that a function of $L/\xi$ with $\xi = c\lvert p - p_c\rvert^{-\nu}$ is a function of $\lvert p - p_c\rvert L^{1/\nu}$, and that keeping the sign of $p - p_c$ requires the variable $(p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$L/\xi = c^{-1}L\lvert p - p_c\rvert^\nu = c^{-1}(L^{1/\nu}\lvert p - p_c\rvert)^\nu$, a function of $\lvert x\rvert$ with $x = (p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}$. Above and below $p_c$ the system is in different phases, so the scaling
function differs on the two sides; using $x$ with its sign encodes both branches in one function.

## Python

Check that two pairs $(p, L)$ with the same $x$ have the same $L/\xi$.

```{.python .run}
nu, pc = 4 / 3, 0.5927
xi = lambda p: abs(p - pc) ** -nu
for p, L in ((0.62, 32), (pc + (0.62 - pc) * (32 / 128) ** (1 / nu), 128)):
    print(f"p = {p:.5f}, L = {L}: x = {(p - pc) * L ** (1 / nu):.4f}, L/xi = {L / xi(p):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p = 0.62000, L = 32: x = 0.3673, L/xi = 0.2630
p = 0.60235, L = 128: x = 0.3673, L/xi = 0.2630
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise checks the relation $D_f = 2 - \beta/\nu$ used in @exm-fss-strength. It follows from finite-size scaling of the strength.

::: {#exr-fss-hyperscaling}
#### The fractal dimension from exponents

Show that if $P_\infty(p_c, L) \propto L^{-\beta/\nu}$ then the largest cluster at $p_c$ has mass $\propto L^{2 - \beta/\nu}$, and evaluate with $\beta = 5/36$, $\nu = 4/3$. Compare with $D_f = 1/(\sigma_p\nu)$ of @exm-perc-fractal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The strength is the mass of the largest cluster over $L^2$, so the mass is $L^2P_\infty \propto L^{2 - \beta/\nu}$. With the exact exponents $2 - 5/48 = 91/48$, and $1/(\sigma_p\nu) = 1/((36/91)(4/3)) = 91/48$: the two relations
agree, as the scaling relations between percolation exponents require.

## Python

The two values as fractions.

```{.python .run}
from fractions import Fraction as F
beta, nu, sigma = F(5, 36), F(4, 3), F(36, 91)
print(2 - beta / nu, 1 / (sigma * nu))
```

```{.text .run-output}
91/48 91/48
```
::::
:::

The last exercise uses finite-size scaling to estimate $\nu$ from the slope of the spanning curves at $p_c$. The derivative $d\Pi_L/dp$ at $p_c$ grows like $L^{1/\nu}$.

::: {#exr-fss-slope}
#### $\nu$ from the steepness

Estimate the slope of $\Pi_L$ at $p_c$ by a central difference with $\Delta p = 0.01$ from $1000$ lattices per point for $L = 16, 32, 64$, and fit $1/\nu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\frac{d}{dp}\Phi((p - p_c)L^{1/\nu}) = L^{1/\nu}\Phi'(0)$ at $p_c$, so the slopes grow like $L^{3/4}$. The finite difference with $\Delta p = 0.01$ is accurate while $0.01L^{3/4}$ is small, but at $L = 64$ it is $0.23$ and the difference quotient averages over the curved part of $\Phi$, underestimating
the slope; the fit gives about $0.67$, below $0.75$. Smaller $\Delta p$ needs many more lattices to beat the noise.

## Python

Central differences of the spanning probability.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, scaling
rng, sizes, slopes = np.random.default_rng(31), (16, 32, 64), []
for L in sizes:
    up, down = (clusters(rng.random((1000, L, L)) < p, kind="spanning").probability for p in (0.6027, 0.5827))
    slopes.append((up - down) / 0.02)
print("slopes:", np.round(slopes, 2).tolist(), f"1/nu = {scaling(np.column_stack([sizes, slopes]), kind="allometric").exponent:.3f}, exact 0.75")
```

```{.text .run-output}
slopes: [6.45, 11.95, 16.35] 1/nu = 0.671, exact 0.75
```
::::
:::
::::

### Real-space renormalisation of percolation

Renormalisation replaces a block of sites by one site and asks how the occupation probability of the block sites depends on that of the original ones. If the map $p \mapsto
R(p)$ describes the same model on a lattice $b$ times coarser, its fixed points are the scale-invariant states, and at a fixed point $p^*$ that repels, a small deviation grows by
the factor $R'(p^*)$ per step while lengths shrink by $b$, which gives $\nu$. Bertin carries this out for the Ising chain by decimation and finds that the only critical fixed point
is at zero temperature [@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 1.4.3, eqs. (1.104)-(1.121)]. For site percolation on the triangular lattice, grouping the sites into triangles of
three and declaring a block occupied when most of its sites are occupied gives a map with a nontrivial fixed point. The block-spin step is written with NumPy, because
`renormalization` of the package coarse-grains networks rather than lattices (issue #30).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-triangular-rg}
#### Renormalisation of triangular-lattice percolation

Group the sites of the triangular lattice into triangles of three sites, which form a triangular lattice with spacing $b = \sqrt3$ times the original, and call a block occupied when at
least two of its sites are occupied. If the sites are occupied independently with probability $p$, the blocks are occupied independently with probability
$$
R(p) = p^3 + 3p^2(1 - p) = 3p^2 - 2p^3 .
$$
(a) The fixed points of $R$ in $[0, 1]$ are $0$, $\frac12$ and $1$; $0$ and $1$ are attracting ($R'(0) = R'(1) = 0$) and $\frac12$ is repelling, with $R'(\frac12) = \frac32$. For $p < \frac12$ the iterates
$R^k(p)$ tend to $0$, and for $p > \frac12$ to $1$.

(b) Suppose the correlation length satisfies $\xi(R(p)) = \xi(p)/b$ in units of the respective lattice spacings, and $\xi(p) \sim c\lvert p - \frac12\rvert^{-\nu}$ near $\frac12$. Then
$$
\nu = \frac{\log b}{\log R'(\tfrac12)} = \frac{\log\sqrt3}{\log\frac32} \approx 1.355 .
$$
:::

::::

*Proof.* The independence of blocks holds because blocks are disjoint sets of sites, and the block probability is the binomial probability of two or three occupied sites out of three.

(a) $R(p) - p = 3p^2 - 2p^3 - p = -p(2p - 1)(p - 1)$, which vanishes exactly at $0, \frac12, 1$. $R'(p) = 6p(1 - p)$, so $R'(0) = R'(1) = 0$ and $R'(\frac12) = \frac32 > 1$. On $(0, \frac12)$, $R(p) - p < 0$ and $R(p)
> 0$, so the iterates decrease and stay positive; they converge to a fixed point in $[0, p)$, which can only be $0$. By the symmetry $R(1 - p) = 1 - R(p)$ (complementing all sites), iterates from $p > \frac12$
converge to $1$.

(b) Write $\delta = p - \frac12$, so $R(p) - \frac12 = \frac32\delta + O(\delta^3)$; the quadratic term vanishes because $R''(\frac12) = 6 - 12\cdot\frac12 = 0$. Then $\xi(R(p)) \sim c(\frac32\lvert\delta\rvert)^{-\nu}$, and the
hypothesis gives $c(\frac32)^{-\nu}\lvert\delta\rvert^{-\nu} \sim c\lvert\delta\rvert^{-\nu}/b$ as $\delta \to 0$, that is $(\frac32)^\nu = b$, which is the formula. $\square$

The fixed point $\frac12$ is the exact threshold of site percolation on the triangular lattice, a consequence of its self-matching property; the exponent $1.355$ is close to the exact $\nu = 4/3 \approx
1.333$ of two-dimensional percolation. The hypothesis of part (b) is what the renormalisation group assumes rather than proves: that the block configuration is again percolation, with no new correlations.
For the majority rule this is not exact, since two blocks can be occupied without their sites being connected, which is why larger blocks are needed to improve the estimate.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The map is easy to iterate. Starting slightly below or above $\frac12$, the occupation flows to the empty or the full lattice, the two trivial fixed points.

::: {#exm-rg-flow}
#### The flow

From $p = 0.45$ the iterates are $0.425, 0.389, 0.336, 0.263, \dots \to 0$; from $p = 0.55$ they mirror these towards $1$. At each step the distance from $\frac12$ grows by about $\frac32$ while lengths shrink by $\sqrt3$.

```{.python .run}
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
for p0 in (0.45, 0.5, 0.55):
    p, orbit = p0, [p0]
    for _ in range(8):
        p = R(p)
        orbit.append(round(p, 4))
    print(p0, orbit)
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.45 [0.45, 0.4253, 0.3887, 0.3358, 0.2626, 0.1706, 0.0774, 0.0171, 0.0009]
0.5 [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]
0.55 [0.55, 0.5748, 0.6113, 0.6642, 0.7374, 0.8294, 0.9226, 0.9829, 0.9991]
```
:::

The correlation length counts the steps to leave the fixed point. Each step multiplies the distance from $\frac12$ by $\frac32$ and divides lengths by $\sqrt3$; reaching distance of order one takes $k \approx
\log(1/\lvert\delta\rvert)/\log\frac32$ steps, a length $b^k = \lvert\delta\rvert^{-\nu}$ in original units.

::: {#exm-rg-xi-counting}
#### Steps to escape

For $\delta = 10^{-3}$, $k = \log(10^3)/\log 1.5 \approx 17$ steps carry the occupation to a distance of order $1$ from $\frac12$, and $b^k = 3^{8.5} \approx 1.1 \times 10^4 = (10^{-3})^{-1.355}$ original spacings: the correlation length.
This is part (b) seen as a count of renormalisation steps.
:::

The Ising chain renormalises to zero temperature. Bertin's decimation of every other spin gives $u' = 4u/(1 + u)^2$ with $u = e^{-4J/T}$, and the only critical fixed point is $u = 0$
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 1.4.3, eqs. (1.117)-(1.121)].

::: {#exm-rg-ising-chain}
#### Decimating the Ising chain

$u = 0$ ($T = 0$) is repelling with $u' \approx 4u$, and $u = 1$ ($T = \infty$) is attracting: every positive temperature flows to infinite temperature, so the chain is disordered at every $T > 0$, the result of
the physics tutorial's transfer matrix ([`exm-crl-ising-chain`](../../fundamentals-of-theoretical-physics/thermodynamics-statistical-mechanics/index.qmd#exm-crl-ising-chain)). The correlation length, which
halves at each step, diverges as $T \to 0$.
:::

Block renormalisation can be done on a real configuration. Applying the majority rule to triangles of a sampled lattice gives a coarser configuration whose occupation is close to $R(p)$.

::: {#exm-rg-sampled}
#### Renormalising a sample

On a triangular lattice represented as a square grid with diagonal neighbours (rows shifted), blocks of three sites in an up-pointing triangle are replaced by their majority. The block occupation of a large sample at
$p = 0.4$ is close to $R(0.4) = 0.352$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng, p = np.random.default_rng(33), 0.4
sites = rng.random((300, 300)) < p
a, b, c = sites[0::2, 0::2], sites[0::2, 1::2], sites[1::2, 0::2]
# scikit-complexity #30: block coarse-graining of a lattice is not in 0.9.0
blocks = (a.astype(int) + b + c) >= 2
print(f"block occupation {blocks.mean():.4f}, R(p) = {3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
block occupation 0.3525, R(p) = 0.3520
```
:::

Larger blocks approach the exact exponent. Blocks of $7$ sites (a hexagon with its centre) with the rule "occupied if the block is spanned" give $\nu$ closer to $4/3$.

::: {#exm-rg-larger-blocks}
#### Bigger blocks

With larger blocks the rule can be "occupied if a cluster spans the block", which respects connectivity better than majority. Estimates of $\nu$ from such cells converge to $4/3$ as the cell size grows,
slowly, because each cell still neglects connections between neighbouring cells.
:::

The square lattice has no exact self-matching block. A $2 \times 2$ block with the rule "occupied if a vertical spanning path exists" gives a fixed point near $0.618$, not the true $0.5927$.

::: {#exm-rg-square}
#### A square block

A $2 \times 2$ block spans vertically if one of its two columns is fully occupied: $R(p) = 2p^2 - p^4$. Its nontrivial fixed point solves $2p - p^3 = 1$, whose root in $(0, 1)$ is $p^* = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2 \approx 0.618$,
and $R'(p^*) = 4p^* - 4p^{*3} \approx 1.528$, so $\nu \approx \log 2/\log 1.528 \approx 1.635$, as an exercise checks.
:::

Universality appears as the independence of $\nu$ from the microscopic details. In the renormalisation picture, models that flow to the same fixed point share exponents; the threshold, which depends on the
starting point of the flow, is not universal.

::: {#exm-rg-universality}
#### Thresholds against exponents

Bond and site percolation on triangular and square lattices have different thresholds (@exm-perc-universality) but flow to the same fixed point of an exact renormalisation, hence the same $\nu = 4/3$. Approximate maps such as
$R$ give approximate fixed points and exponents, but the structure, a repelling fixed point between two attracting ones, is the same for all.
:::

The renormalisation group explains finite-size scaling. A lattice of side $L$ renormalises in $k$ steps to one of side $Lb^{-k}$, and the deviation $\delta$ to $\delta(\frac32)^k$; after $\log_bL$ steps the system is
one block, and its state depends only on $\delta(\frac32)^{\log_bL} = \delta L^{1/\nu}$, the scaling variable of @def-finite-size-scaling.

::: {#exm-rg-fss}
#### From renormalisation to scaling

With $(\frac32)^{\log_bL} = L^{\log(3/2)/\log b} = L^{1/\nu}$, the spanning probability of an $L \times L$ system becomes $\Pi_L(p) = \Phi((p - \frac12)L^{1/\nu})$, the hypothesis of finite-size scaling, derived here from
the map $R$.
:::

The renormalisation idea goes back to Kadanoff's blocks of spins. Bertin presents it as defocusing a picture until fine details blur, keeping the large-scale properties
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 1.4.3].

::: {#exm-rg-defocusing}
#### Defocusing

At $p$ below $\frac12$ each defocusing makes the picture emptier, above it fuller, and at exactly $\frac12$ it looks the same at every resolution, the statistical self-similarity of the critical cluster. The fixed point
is the mathematical form of the scale invariance of @thm-scale-invariance.
:::

Counting renormalisation steps also estimates the correlation length. Near the fixed point the deviation grows by the factor $R'(\frac12) = \frac32$ per step while lengths shrink by $b = \sqrt3$, so the
number of steps needed for the deviation to become of order one measures, in blocks, how far correlations reach.

::: {#exm-rg-correlation-length}
#### Steps to leave the fixed point

Start at $p = 0.45$, so $\delta = -0.05$. In the linear approximation the deviation reaches order one after $k = \log 20/\log 1.5 \approx 7.39$ steps, at which point a block is of side $b^k = \sqrt3^{\,7.39}
\approx 58$ lattice spacings. This equals $\lvert\delta\rvert^{-\nu} = 20^{1.355} \approx 58$, since $b^k = \lvert\delta\rvert^{-\log b/\log(3/2)}$: the correlation length diverges like $\lvert p -
p_c\rvert^{-\nu}$ with the exponent of the proposition.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the formula for $R$ by enumerating the eight configurations of a block. It is the binomial computation of the proof.

::: {#exr-rg-enumerate}
#### The block probability

Enumerate the configurations of three sites, mark those with a majority occupied, and add their probabilities at $p = 0.3$; compare with $3p^2 - 2p^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Three configurations have exactly two occupied sites, each with probability $p^2(1 - p)$, and one has three, with $p^3$; the sum is $3p^2(1 - p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3$, $0.216$ at $p = 0.3$.

## Python

The enumeration.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
p = 0.3
total = sum(p ** sum(c) * (1 - p) ** (3 - sum(c)) for c in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=3) if sum(c) >= 2)
print(round(total, 6), round(3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3, 6))
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.216 0.216
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves the symmetry $R(1 - p) = 1 - R(p)$ used in part (a). It says that complementing all sites maps the occupied majority to the empty majority.

::: {#exr-rg-symmetry}
#### Particle-hole symmetry

Show $R(1 - p) = 1 - R(p)$ algebraically and by the complement argument, and deduce that the orbit from $1 - p$ is the mirror of the orbit from $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A block has an occupied majority iff its complement has an empty majority; with occupation $1 - p$ the complement has occupation $p$, so $R(1 - p) = 1 - R(p)$. Algebraically, $3(1 - p)^2 - 2(1 - p)^3 = (1 - p)^2(1 + 2p) = 1 - 3p^2 + 2p^3$.
By induction $R^k(1 - p) = 1 - R^k(p)$.

## Python

The identity on a grid of $p$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
p = np.linspace(0, 1, 11)
print(float(np.abs(R(1 - p) - (1 - R(p))).max()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
2.220446049250313e-16
```
::::
:::

The third exercise computes $\nu$ from the iteration itself rather than from the derivative. It counts the steps needed to reach a fixed distance from $\frac12$.

::: {#exr-rg-count-steps}
#### $\nu$ from step counts

For $\delta = 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}, \dots, 10^{-6}$, count the steps $k(\delta)$ until $R^k(\frac12 + \delta) > 0.9$, and fit $\nu$ from $b^{k} \propto \delta^{-\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Near the fixed point each step multiplies $\delta$ by $\frac32$, so $k \approx \log(c/\delta)/\log\frac32$ and $b^k \approx (c/\delta)^{\log b/\log 1.5} = (c/\delta)^\nu$. The slope of $k\log b$ against $\log(1/\delta)$ is $\nu$, up to the
rounding of $k$ to an integer.

## Python

Step counts and the fitted slope.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
deltas, steps = 10.0 ** -np.arange(2, 7), []
for d in deltas:
    p, k = 0.5 + d, 0
    while p <= 0.9:
        p, k = R(p), k + 1
    steps.append(k)
print("steps:", steps, f"nu = {np.polyfit(np.log(1 / deltas), np.array(steps) * np.log(np.sqrt(3)), 1)[0]:.3f}, formula {np.log(np.sqrt(3)) / np.log(1.5):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
steps: [10, 16, 22, 27, 33] nu = 1.360, formula 1.355
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise solves the square block of @exm-rg-square. Its fixed point is the inverse golden ratio.

::: {#exr-rg-square}
#### The $2 \times 2$ block

Show that a $2 \times 2$ block spans vertically with probability $R(p) = 2p^2 - p^4$, that the nontrivial fixed point is $p^* = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2$, and compute $\nu = \log 2/\log R'(p^*)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A vertical path exists iff a column is full; each column is full with probability $p^2$, so $R = 1 - (1 - p^2)^2 = 2p^2 - p^4$. Fixed points: $p(2p - p^3 - 1) = 0$, and $p^3 - 2p + 1 = (p - 1)(p^2 + p - 1)$ gives $p = 1$ and $p^* = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2
\approx 0.618$. $R'(p^*) = 4p^* - 4p^{*3}$, about $1.528$, and $\nu = \log 2/\log 1.528 \approx 1.635$, further from $4/3$ than the triangular block.

## Python

The fixed point and the exponent by root finding.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq
R = lambda p: 2 * p**2 - p**4
p_star = brentq(lambda p: R(p) - p, 0.3, 0.9)
slope = 4 * p_star - 4 * p_star**3
print(f"p* = {p_star:.6f}, (sqrt5 - 1)/2 = {(5**0.5 - 1) / 2:.6f}, R'(p*) = {slope:.4f}, nu = {np.log(2) / np.log(slope):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p* = 0.618034, (sqrt5 - 1)/2 = 0.618034, R'(p*) = 1.5279, nu = 1.6353
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise solves Bertin's recursion for the Ising chain. It locates the fixed points and checks the stability claims of @exm-rg-ising-chain.

::: {#exr-rg-ising-chain}
#### Bertin's recursion

Show that $u' = 4u/(1 + u)^2$ has fixed points $0$ and $1$ in $[0, 1]$, that $u = 0$ is repelling and $u = 1$ attracting, and that every $u \in (0, 1)$ flows to $1$. Iterate from $u = 10^{-4}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$u = 4u/(1 + u)^2$ gives $u = 0$ or $(1 + u)^2 = 4$, $u = 1$ in $[0, 1]$. The derivative $4(1 - u)/(1 + u)^3$ is $4$ at $0$ (repelling) and $0$ at $1$ (attracting). For $0 < u < 1$, $u' - u = u(3 - 2u - u^2)/(1 + u)^2 = u(1 - u)(3 + u)/(1 + u)^2 > 0$
and $u' \leq 1$ (since $4u \leq (1 + u)^2$), so the iterates increase to a fixed point in $(0, 1]$, which is $1$ [@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, eqs. (1.120)-(1.121)].

## Python

The orbit from a low temperature.

```{.python .run}
u, orbit = 1e-4, []
for _ in range(12):
    u = 4 * u / (1 + u) ** 2
    orbit.append(f"{u:.4g}")
print(orbit)
```

```{.text .run-output}
['0.0003999', '0.001598', '0.006373', '0.02517', '0.0958', '0.3191', '0.7336', '0.9764', '0.9999', '1', '1', '1']
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks the independence of blocks claimed in the proof, on a sample. Neighbouring blocks share no site, so their occupations are independent.

::: {#exr-rg-independence}
#### Independent blocks

For the sampled blocks of @exm-rg-sampled at $p = 0.5$, compute the correlation between horizontally adjacent blocks and the share of occupied blocks. Explain why independence does not mean that block clusters equal site
clusters.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Disjoint blocks are functions of disjoint sets of independent sites, so they are independent: the correlation is zero up to noise, and the occupation is $R(\frac12) = \frac12$. But two adjacent occupied blocks need not have
connected majorities, and an unoccupied block can still carry a connection through its single occupied site; the block configuration has the right law but the wrong connectivity, the approximation of part (b).

## Python

The block correlation and occupation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
sites = np.random.default_rng(34).random((600, 600)) < 0.5
# scikit-complexity #30: block coarse-graining of a lattice is not in 0.9.0
blocks = (sites[0::2, 0::2].astype(int) + sites[0::2, 1::2] + sites[1::2, 0::2]) >= 2
x, y = blocks[:, :-1].ravel(), blocks[:, 1:].ravel()
print(f"occupation {blocks.mean():.4f}, correlation of neighbours {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
occupation 0.5001, correlation of neighbours 0.0043
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares the renormalised exponent with the exact one in the scaling of the spanning probability. With $\nu = 1.355$ and $\nu = 4/3$ the collapse of @exm-fss-spanning-curves hardly differs.

::: {#exr-rg-collapse}
#### Does $1.355$ collapse the data?

Using spanning curves of square-lattice percolation for $L = 16, 32, 64$, compare the quality of the collapse at $p_c = 0.5927$ with $\nu = 4/3$, $1.355$ and $1.635$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The exponent is universal, so the square lattice has the same $\nu = 4/3$ as the triangular lattice, and the triangular estimate $1.355$ is within $2\%$ of it. On these lattices, however,
the quality measure barely distinguishes even $1.635$: changing $1/\nu$ from $0.75$ to $0.61$ rescales the variable $x$ of the largest lattice relative to the smallest by $4^{0.14} \approx 1.2$, and the
curves are steep and noisy enough near $p_c$ to absorb this. Exponents are hard to measure by collapse over a small range of sizes, which is why the renormalisation estimate and the exact value
matter; telling $1.355$ from $4/3$ would need lattices hundreds of times larger.

## Python

The quality at three values of $\nu$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters, data_collapse
rng, ps = np.random.default_rng(35), np.round(np.linspace(0.54, 0.64, 11), 3)
curves = {L: np.array([clusters(rng.random((400, L, L)) < p, kind="spanning").probability for p in ps]) for L in (16, 32, 64)}
for nu in (4 / 3, 1.355, 1.635):
    print(f"nu = {nu:.3f}: quality {data_collapse(curves, parameters=ps, critical=0.5927, nu=nu).quality:.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
nu = 1.333: quality 0.00370
nu = 1.355: quality 0.00358
nu = 1.635: quality 0.00358
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise renormalises the spanning probability itself. Iterating the triangular map from $p$ gives the occupation of a single block representing a lattice of $3^k$ sites, a crude estimate of $\Pi$.

::: {#exr-rg-spanning}
#### Spanning from the map

Interpret $R^k(p)$ as the probability that a system of $3^k$ sites is "occupied at the largest scale". Compute it for $k = 2, 4, 6$ and $p = 0.45, 0.5, 0.55$, and explain how it sharpens into a step at $\frac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a), $R^k(p) \to 0$ for $p < \frac12$ and $\to 1$ for $p > \frac12$, with $R^k(\frac12) = \frac12$ for all $k$: a sequence of curves that cross at $\frac12$ and sharpen, the behaviour of $\Pi_L$ in @exm-fss-spanning-curves. The width
shrinks by $\frac32$ per step, like $L^{-1/\nu}$ with $L = 3^{k/2}$.

## Python

The iterated map at three values of $p$.

```{.python .run}
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
for k in (2, 4, 6):
    values = []
    for p in (0.45, 0.5, 0.55):
        q = p
        for _ in range(k):
            q = R(q)
        values.append(round(q, 4))
    print(f"k = {k}: {values}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 2: [0.3887, 0.5, 0.6113]
k = 4: [0.2626, 0.5, 0.7374]
k = 6: [0.0774, 0.5, 0.9226]
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise looks at the stability of the trivial fixed points. Near $p = 0$ the map is quadratic, so the flow to the empty lattice is superexponentially fast.

::: {#exr-rg-trivial}
#### Flow to the empty lattice

Show that $R(p) \leq 3p^2$, so $R^k(p) \leq \frac13(3p)^{2^k}$, and interpret: the correlation length of the renormalised lattice decreases quickly to zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$R(p) = 3p^2 - 2p^3 \leq 3p^2$. If $q_k \leq \frac13(3p)^{2^k}$ then $q_{k + 1} \leq 3q_k^2 \leq \frac13(3p)^{2^{k + 1}}$. For $p < \frac13$ this falls doubly exponentially: after a few steps the renormalised lattice is empty at every scale, so the
original lattice has no correlations beyond a few blocks.

## Python

The iterates against the bound from $p = 0.2$.

```{.python .run}
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
q = 0.2
for k in range(1, 5):
    q = R(q)
    print(k, f"{q:.3e}", f"{(3 * 0.2) ** (2**k) / 3:.3e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 1.040e-01 1.200e-01
2 3.020e-02 4.320e-02
3 2.681e-03 5.599e-03
4 2.152e-05 9.404e-05
```
::::
:::

The last exercise applies the renormalisation to a sampled configuration twice. The block occupation after two steps should follow $R(R(p))$ at the critical point and away from it.

::: {#exr-rg-two-steps}
#### Two renormalisation steps

Renormalise a $1200 \times 1200$ sample twice with the block rule of @exm-rg-sampled at $p = 0.45, 0.5, 0.55$, and compare the final occupations with $R(R(p))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The first step produces independent blocks with occupation $R(p)$, so the second step, applied to them, produces $R(R(p))$ exactly in law. The sample values agree within the noise of a few thousand blocks, and they show the
flow away from $\frac12$ of part (a).

## Python

Two steps of the block rule.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
R = lambda p: 3 * p**2 - 2 * p**3
step = lambda s: (s[0::2, 0::2].astype(int) + s[0::2, 1::2] + s[1::2, 0::2]) >= 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(36)
for p in (0.45, 0.5, 0.55):
    s = step(step(rng.random((1200, 1200)) < p))
    print(f"p = {p}: two steps {s.mean():.4f}, R(R(p)) = {R(R(p)):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p = 0.45: two steps 0.3889, R(R(p)) = 0.3887
p = 0.5: two steps 0.5041, R(R(p)) = 0.5000
p = 0.55: two steps 0.6116, R(R(p)) = 0.6113
```
::::
:::
::::

## Absorbing-state transitions {#sec-absorbing-states}

Equilibrium transitions separate two phases that both fluctuate. Many processes of complex systems have instead a state that, once reached, is never left: an epidemic with no infected
individuals, a chemical reaction without catalyst, a sandpile without unstable sites, a population that has died out. Such absorbing states make the dynamics irreversible, so no Boltzmann
distribution describes them, yet they show sharp transitions between an absorbing phase and an active phase, with critical exponents and universality classes of their own
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 3.2.2; @grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 6.4.1]. The prominent class is directed percolation, whose name comes from reading the active sites
of a $d$-dimensional process in time as clusters of a $(d + 1)$-dimensional percolation problem with a preferred direction. This section defines the contact process, the standard lattice
model, and proves the mean-field theory of absorbing transitions, which gives the exponents above the upper critical dimension. The fully connected stochastic version, where
fluctuations always lead to absorption, is the birth-death process of @prp-birth-death and the absorbing example of @sec-master-equation.

For more on this topic, see @bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021 [Secs. 3.2.2-3.2.3] and @grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015 [Sec. 6.4.1].

### The contact process

The contact process is an epidemic on a lattice without immunity. Infected sites recover spontaneously and infect their neighbours; the healthy lattice is absorbing, because without infected
sites nothing happens. The definition fixes the rates and the order parameter. It forgets everything about real diseases except the competition between local spreading and recovery, which is
enough for a transition.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-contact-process}
#### Contact process and absorbing-state transition

The **contact process** on a graph with $z$ neighbours per site is the continuous-time Markov chain on configurations $\eta \in \{0, 1\}^V$ (healthy or infected) in which each infected site
becomes healthy at rate $1$, and each healthy site becomes infected at rate $\lambda n/z$, where $n$ is the number of its infected neighbours; $\lambda$ is the **infection rate**. The all-healthy
configuration is **absorbing**: the chain never leaves it. On an infinite lattice, the **density of active sites** $\rho(t)$, the mean share of infected sites, and the **survival probability**
$P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t)$, the probability that the process started from one infected site is not yet absorbed at time $t$, are the order parameters. The process has an **absorbing-state
transition** at $\lambda_c$ if $\lim_{t \to \infty}P_{\mathrm{surv}}(t) = 0$ for $\lambda < \lambda_c$ and $> 0$ for $\lambda > \lambda_c$; the critical behaviour is described by $\rho_{\mathrm{st}} \propto
(\lambda - \lambda_c)^\beta$ and by a correlation time $\tau \propto \lvert\lambda - \lambda_c\rvert^{-\nu_\parallel}$.
:::

::::

On the square lattice $\lambda_c = 1.64872(3)$ with this normalisation, against $3.2978$ on the chain [@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Sec. 11.1, eq. (11.1) and Table 11.1], and `ContactProcessSystem` documents a critical rate near $1.65$; it advances time in slices of length $\tau$ (its parameter
`tau`, the length of one step), not the correlation time. On any finite lattice the absorbing state is reached with probability one, as for every finite chain with an absorbing state reachable
from everywhere, so the active phase is a long-lived metastable state whose lifetime grows exponentially with the size.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Below the critical rate the infection dies out. At $\lambda = 1.2$ on a $32 \times 32$ lattice started half infected, the density falls to near zero within a few hundred units of time.

::: {#exm-cp-three-rates}
#### Three infection rates

The density at three rates on a $64 \times 64$ lattice: decay to zero below $\lambda_c$, slow decay near it, a stationary active density above.
@fig-contact-process compares the runs with the mean-field solution of the same rates, which relaxes much faster and to higher densities.

![Density of infected sites of the contact process on a $64 \times 64$ lattice at three infection rates (solid), against the mean-field solution at the same rates (dashed). Below the
critical rate the lattice process dies out although mean field predicts an active state.](figures/contact_process.svg){#fig-contact-process width=70%}

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import ContactProcessSystem
for rate in (1.4, 1.65, 1.9):
    rho = np.asarray(simulate(ContactProcessSystem((64, 64), rate=rate, random_state=4), until=500, random_state=4).get_values("lattice.infected")).reshape(501, -1).mean(axis=1)
    print(f"lambda = {rate}: density at t = 0, 100, 200, 500: {rho[[0, 100, 200, 500]].round(4).tolist()}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 1.4: density at t = 0, 100, 200, 500: [0.4961, 0.1482, 0.0645, 0.0117]
lambda = 1.65: density at t = 0, 100, 200, 500: [0.4961, 0.2542, 0.1919, 0.1665]
lambda = 1.9: density at t = 0, 100, 200, 500: [0.4961, 0.3518, 0.3289, 0.3184]
```
:::

The process is a sum of independent infections only in mean field. On a lattice the infected sites are clustered, and an infected site surrounded by infected neighbours cannot spread, which raises
the threshold above the mean-field value $1$.

::: {#exm-cp-why-above-one}
#### Why $\lambda_c > 1$ on a lattice

In mean field an infected site meets healthy neighbours in proportion to the global healthy density; on a lattice its neighbours are often already infected, because infection spreads locally.
Each infection is then less productive than mean field assumes, and a higher rate, $1.65$ instead of $1$, is needed to sustain the process.
:::

Bertin's reaction-diffusion model is the particle version. Particles branch $A \to 2A$ at rate $\kappa$, die $A \to \emptyset$ at rate $\nu$, annihilate $2A \to A$ at rate $\lambda$, and diffuse
[@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 3.2.2, eqs. (3.28)-(3.31)].

::: {#exm-cp-reaction-diffusion}
#### Branching and annihilation

Its mean-field equation $\partial_t\rho = (\kappa - \nu)\rho - \lambda\rho^2 + D\nabla^2\rho$ has the same structure as the contact process: linear growth against a quadratic saturation. The control
parameter is $\varepsilon = \kappa - \nu$, and the transition is at $\varepsilon = 0$ in mean field; both models belong to the directed percolation class.
:::

The fully connected version has no space and keeps the fluctuations. `AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem` runs Bertin's three reactions with $N$ particles in a volume $V$, which is the master equation of
@sec-master-equation.

::: {#exm-cp-fully-connected}
#### Fluctuations in a finite volume

At $\kappa = 2$, $\nu = 1$, $\lambda = 1$ and $V = 50$ the deterministic fixed point is $\rho_0 = 1$, $N \approx 50$, and the number of particles fluctuates around it, with relative size $\frac{\lambda}{\kappa - \nu}\sqrt{\kappa/(\lambda V)} \approx
0.2$ according to the documentation; absorption happens only after an exponentially long time.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem
n = np.asarray(simulate(AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem(kappa=2.0, nu=1.0, lam=1.0, volume=50.0), until=200, random_state=1).get_values("particles.n"))
print(f"mean N {n[100:].mean():.1f}, relative fluctuation {n[100:].std() / n[100:].mean():.3f}, predicted {np.sqrt(2 / 50):.3f}, minimum {int(n.min())}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean N 50.3, relative fluctuation 0.207, predicted 0.200, minimum 22
```
:::

The fixed-energy sandpile is Gros's example of an absorbing transition. Without drive and without loss, the number of grains is conserved, and the density of grains decides whether topplings stop
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 6.4.1, Fig. 6.9].

::: {#exm-cp-sandpile}
#### A conserved sandpile

`FixedEnergySandpileSystem` topples every site with at least four grains. Below a critical density near $2.125$ the activity stops in an absorbing configuration; above it the pile stays active.
Gros explains self-organised criticality as a slow drive and a fast dissipation that pin the density at this critical value.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.criticality import FixedEnergySandpileSystem
for density in (1.9, 2.3):
    run = simulate(FixedEnergySandpileSystem((32, 32), density=density, random_state=5), until=2000, random_state=5)
    h = np.asarray(run.get_values("pile.height")).reshape(2001, -1)
    print(f"density {density}: active sites at t = 2000: {int((h[-1] >= 4).sum())}, grains conserved: {bool(h[0].sum() == h[-1].sum())}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
density 1.9: active sites at t = 2000: 0, grains conserved: True
density 2.3: active sites at t = 2000: 181, grains conserved: True
```
:::

Directed percolation explains the name of the class. Draw the infected sites of a one-dimensional contact process in a space-time diagram; an infection is passed only forward in time, so active sites form
clusters connected along a preferred direction.

::: {#exm-cp-directed}
#### Space-time clusters

In discrete time with infection probability $p$ per bond, the set of sites reachable from one initial infection is a cluster of directed bond percolation on a tilted square lattice; survival forever means an infinite
directed cluster. The threshold is $p_c \approx 0.6447$ in $1 + 1$ dimensions, and the exponent $\beta = 0.2767$ there, $0.580$ in $2 + 1$ dimensions, differs from the mean-field value $1$
[@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Sec. 11.1, Fig. 11.1 and Table 11.1].
:::

Absorbing transitions also govern epidemics on networks. The contact process with an absorbing healthy state is the SIS epidemic of later chapters on networks, with $\lambda$ the ratio of infection and
recovery rates.

::: {#exm-cp-epidemic}
#### An epidemic threshold

On a fully mixed population, mean field gives the threshold $\lambda_c = 1$, the basic reproduction number $R_0 = \lambda$ crossing $1$. Below it the disease dies out, above it an endemic state persists with
prevalence $1 - 1/\lambda$, which the proposition of this section proves.
:::

The survival probability distinguishes the phases on large lattices. Started from a single infected site, the process dies quickly below $\lambda_c$, survives with positive probability above.

::: {#exm-cp-survival}
#### Survival from one site

From one infected site at the centre of a large lattice, the share of runs still active after $t$ steps decays to $0$ below $\lambda_c$ and levels off above. At $\lambda_c$ it decays like $t^{-\delta}$, with $\delta
= 0.4510$ in two dimensions and $\delta = 1$ in mean field [@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Table 11.1].
:::

The universality of directed percolation is a conjecture with wide support [@bottcherComputationalStatisticalPhysics2021, Sec. 11.1]. Janssen and Grassberger conjectured that absorbing transitions with a single absorbing state, short-range interactions and no
conservation law belong to it; Bertin mentions that systems with conservation laws form other classes [@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 3.2.2].

::: {#exm-cp-universality}
#### Classes of absorbing transitions

The contact process, Bertin's branching-annihilation process and directed bond percolation share the exponents $(\beta, \nu_\perp, \nu_\parallel)$ of directed percolation; the fixed-energy sandpile, which conserves grains,
does not. The upper critical dimension is $4$, above which mean field is exact [@bertinStatisticalPhysicsComplex2021, Sec. 3.2.2].
:::

Experiments with absorbing transitions are rare because absorbing states are fragile. Any spontaneous source of activity destroys them, which Bertin's parameter $\epsilon$ in `AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem` models.

::: {#exm-cp-spontaneous}
#### A spontaneous source

With a small rate $\epsilon$ of particle creation in the empty state, the empty state is no longer absorbing, and the stationary distribution exists and has mass near $0$ and near $\rho_0$ (Bertin's Exercise 3.3,
documented in `AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem`). The sharp transition is rounded, as a field rounds the Ising transition.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise shows that a finite contact process is absorbed with probability one. It is the argument behind the metastability remark after the definition.

::: {#exr-cp-finite-absorption}
#### Absorption is certain on a finite graph

For the contact process on a finite graph with $N$ sites, show that from any configuration the probability of absorption within time $1$ is at least $c > 0$ independent of the configuration, and deduce that absorption is
certain. Check on a $4 \times 4$ lattice at $\lambda = 2$, above the threshold of the infinite lattice, that runs die, and see how much longer they last at $\lambda = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Use the exponential clocks of the chain. The total infection rate never exceeds $\lambda N$, so with probability at least $e^{-\lambda N}$ no infection event occurs in $[0, 1]$; independently, each of the at most $N$
infected sites has its recovery clock ring before time $1$ with probability $1 - e^{-1}$. On the intersection of these events the configuration is healthy at time $1$, so absorption within time $1$ has probability at least
$c = e^{-\lambda N}(1 - e^{-1})^N > 0$ from every configuration. By the Markov property, $\mathbb P(\text{not absorbed by time } k) \leq (1 - c)^k \to 0$. The time can be astronomically long: $c$ is exponentially small in $N$.

## Python

The lifetimes of $20$ runs on a $4 \times 4$ lattice at the two rates, capped at $3000$ steps.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import ContactProcessSystem
for rate in (2.0, 3.0):
    lifetimes = []
    for seed in range(20):
        rho = np.asarray(simulate(ContactProcessSystem((4, 4), rate=rate, random_state=seed), until=3000, random_state=seed).get_values("lattice.infected")).reshape(3001, -1).mean(axis=1)
        dead = np.flatnonzero(rho == 0)
        lifetimes.append(int(dead[0]) if dead.size else 3000)
    print(f"lambda = {rate}: median lifetime {int(np.median(lifetimes))} steps, runs alive at 3000: {lifetimes.count(3000)} of 20")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 2.0: median lifetime 293 steps, runs alive at 3000: 0 of 20
lambda = 3.0: median lifetime 3000 steps, runs alive at 3000: 11 of 20
```
::::
:::

The second exercise derives the mean-field equation of the contact process. It replaces the number of infected neighbours by its mean.

::: {#exr-cp-mean-field}
#### The mean-field equation

Show that if neighbours are independent with infection probability $\rho$, the density obeys $\dot\rho = \lambda\rho(1 - \rho) - \rho$, and find its fixed points and their stability.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A healthy site (density $1 - \rho$) has on average $z\rho$ infected neighbours and becomes infected at rate $\lambda\rho$; infected sites recover at rate $1$. So $\dot\rho = \lambda\rho(1 - \rho) - \rho = (\lambda - 1)\rho - \lambda\rho^2$, Bertin's equation
with $\varepsilon = \lambda - 1$ and annihilation rate $\lambda$. Fixed points $0$ and $1 - 1/\lambda$; the derivative at $0$ is $\lambda - 1$, so $0$ is stable for $\lambda < 1$ and unstable above, where $1 - 1/\lambda$ is
stable, a transcritical bifurcation (@def-bifurcation).

## Python

The equation integrated at three rates.

```{.python .run}
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import DynamicalSystem
for lam in (0.8, 1.0, 1.5):
    field = DynamicalSystem(states={"rho": 0.5}, parameters={"lam": lam}, element="cp",
                            equations={"rho": lambda s: s.target.lam * s.target.rho * (1 - s.target.rho) - s.target.rho})
    rho = simulate(field, until=200, dt=200).get_values("cp.rho")[-1]
    print(f"lambda = {lam}: rho(200) = {round(float(rho), 4) + 0.0:.4f}, fixed point {max(0.0, 1 - 1 / lam):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 0.8: rho(200) = 0.0000, fixed point 0.0000
lambda = 1.0: rho(200) = 0.0050, fixed point 0.0000
lambda = 1.5: rho(200) = 0.3333, fixed point 0.3333
```
::::
:::

The third exercise estimates the critical rate of the contact process from the density at a fixed time. Above the threshold the density stays positive, below it decays, and the change brackets $\lambda_c$.

::: {#exr-cp-threshold}
#### Bracketing $\lambda_c$

On a $64 \times 64$ lattice, compute the density at $t = 1000$ for $\lambda = 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8$, and bracket the critical rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Below $\lambda_c$ the density decays exponentially and is essentially $0$ by $t = 1000$; above it it settles at a positive value that grows with $\lambda - \lambda_c$. The density drops steeply between $1.7$ and $1.5$, consistent with
$\lambda_c \approx 1.65$; near the threshold the decay is a slow power law, so at $t = 1000$ the densities at $1.5$ and $1.6$ have not yet reached zero, and the bracket is only as sharp as the run is long.

## Python

Densities at $t = 1000$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import ContactProcessSystem
for rate in (1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8):
    rho = np.asarray(simulate(ContactProcessSystem((64, 64), rate=rate, random_state=6), until=1000, random_state=6).get_values("lattice.infected"))[-1].mean()
    print(f"lambda = {rate}: rho(1000) = {rho:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 1.5: rho(1000) = 0.0146
lambda = 1.6: rho(1000) = 0.0950
lambda = 1.7: rho(1000) = 0.2188
lambda = 1.8: rho(1000) = 0.3215
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise compares the stationary density with mean field. Mean field predicts $1 - 1/\lambda$, which overestimates the lattice density at every rate.

::: {#exr-cp-stationary}
#### Stationary density against mean field

For $\lambda = 2, 3, 5$ on a $64 \times 64$ lattice, compute the stationary density (averaged over $t = 300$ to $600$) and compare with $1 - 1/\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The clustering of infected sites (@exm-cp-why-above-one) reduces the effective infection rate, so the lattice density is below $1 - 1/\lambda$; the gap shrinks at large $\lambda$, where almost all neighbours of a healthy site are
infected anyway and mean field becomes accurate.

## Python

Stationary densities.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import ContactProcessSystem
for rate in (2.0, 3.0, 5.0):
    rho = np.asarray(simulate(ContactProcessSystem((64, 64), rate=rate, random_state=7), until=600, random_state=7).get_values("lattice.infected")).reshape(601, -1).mean(axis=1)[300:].mean()
    print(f"lambda = {rate}: lattice {rho:.4f}, mean field {1 - 1 / rate:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 2.0: lattice 0.3741, mean field 0.5000
lambda = 3.0: lattice 0.6078, mean field 0.6667
lambda = 5.0: lattice 0.7571, mean field 0.8000
```
